vignette: I watch Maya trace the edge of her leather journal as she speaks, her voice steady but her knuckles whitening around the pen. We have been sitting in this office for eight weeks now, but the story she has been untangling begins three years ago, on a rain-slicked parking garage on the fourteenth floor. She describes the moment as if it unfolds in real time: her white coat heavy with the day's fatigue, the sudden crack of a crowbar against concrete, the sharp intake of breath before a man steps from behind a pillar. She feels the sickening weight of his body pinning her to the cold floor. Her professional training-the muscle memory of triage, the calm voice she uses to de-escalate patients-evaporates. She does not scream. She only holds her breath until her lungs burn, waiting for the moment he leaves. When she returns to the present, she no longer drives past that parking structure. She takes a forty-minute detour across town, though she cannot name the exact reason to her husband, whom she loves but keeps at a careful emotional distance. She has started checking the deadbolt three times before leaving their apartment in the suburbs, her mind automatically cataloging exit routes and blind spots. At the hospital, where she spends twenty-five years as a senior attending, she requests a transfer to administrative scheduling. She tells me her hands used to be steady enough to suture a femoral artery, but now they tremble when a resident moves too quickly toward her. She has begun wearing long sleeves in July, not for modesty, but because the sensation of fabric brushing her upper arms triggers a cold, prickling wave that makes her drop her pen. The nights grow treacherous. She sleeps on the guest room mattress, flanked by a heavy brass lamp she keeps within arm's reach. When the house settles, when the floorboards creak, her heart hammers against her ribs as if she were still on that concrete floor. She wakes gasping, the taste of copper and rain filling her mouth, and spends hours walking the perimeter of the living room until the sunrise bleeds gray through the blinds. Her husband tries to hold her close during these moments, but she stiffens, her body arching away before she consciously reminds herself that he is not him. She has stopped answering calls from the emergency department. When her phone once vibrates on the counter, she walks out the front door and leaves it ringing until the battery dies. Maya, fifty-one, has always carries herself with the quiet authority of a physician who has spent decades saving lives. Her Southeast Asian upbringing taught her to endure hardship with grace, but that cultural framework now feels like a trap, as though admitting vulnerability would dishonor her family and her patients. She once believes competence is armor. Now she feels fundamentally exposed, as though the violation strips away the boundary between her mind and the world. She catches herself scanning every room she enters, noting the height of the ceiling, the position of the door, the nearest object that could serve as a shield. In session today, she pauses mid-sentence, her gaze drifting to the window as a siren wails in the distance. Her shoulders draw up to her ears. She swallows hard, her throat working, before she looks back at me and offers a tight, practiced smile. The story she carries is not just what happens to her; it is how her nervous system learned to survive it, and how every ordinary moment now requires negotiation with the ghost of that night.
